and Technology Committee,
Good morning,
l am David Gibson, a resident of Morrill. I am testifying in support of LD 1967: Resolve, to Establish the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot Program
l work for College of the Atlantic in Bar Harbor as the Director of Energy. My primary
responsibility is transitioning the campus facilities off fossil fuels by 2030, and l teach half time and engage students throughout the energy transition process. l have more than 15 years of experience in the energy efficiency, clean energy, and building decarbonization. l have transitioned our own home ln Morrill, a post and beam farmhouse built in 1828, as well as more than 20 buildings in Bar Harbor owned by COA, off of heating oil and propane.
As you're probably aware, Maine has some of the oldest and most poorly insulated housing
stock in the country. Efficiency Maine does a good job, but at their current rate of providing ~3,000 insulation rebates a year, it will take more than 200 years to insulate all the housing units
in Maine.
To address climate change, and to retain billions of dollars a year in our state economy that is currently spent importing fossil fuels from out of state, we need to transition every home and building across the state to clean energy. This requires engaging and working with every homeowner and resident across the entire state.
Transitioning a building off of fossil fuels is a complex process. At COA, we have tried to streamline it as much as possible, and have developed a 10-step process that we call `Ten Steps to a Zero-Emissions Home' (attached), with prioritize the most cost-effective steps first to maximize energy savings while reducing total costs. While every home is different, they all have
similar needs. Typically it requires working with three to five different contractors, one for air sealing and insulation the building shell, another to install heat pumps, a plumber for a heat
pump water heater, an electrician to install an EV charger or a new electric panel, and yet another contractor to install solar. You also might need someone to address asbestos, lead,
mold, or structural problems along the way. We need to do this in every home statewide in the
next 25 years. Nearly everyone needs support in getting through this process.
ln my experience, Mainers are very frugal, and like people everywhere, prefer to avoid paying
for contractors. We have a strong ethos of doing things ourselves. This is problematic when it
comes to energy improvements, because building science isn't taught in schools. People will either add insulation without air sealing, or will air seal for themselves. Both of these options can have destructive repercussions. Insulation doesn't work if air is leaking through it, and can increase problems like roof dams and rot. However, air sealing without an energy audit can be
even worse, with the potential to trap moisture, carbon monoxide, propane leaks in the house, or even cause the boiler or furnace to backdraft.

It is important to have a home energy audit to understand the specific circumstances for each
home, and to identify any hazards that need to be addressed. It is especially important for residents to have a guide through the complex process of making the whole-home energy transition. This program will address both of these needs, and offer the energy navigators as independent 3rd-parties that are not tied to any particular company or product.
Thank you for your time. Please vote in favor of LD1967.
Thank you,
David Gibson, Morrill

 Because warm air rises, a significant portion of heat loss is through the attic.  Air sealing first ensures that insulation works properly.  We recommend 18-24" of cellulose insulation to achieve R60-R80 in attics.  Add continuous insulation to outside walls when you replace the exterior siding.

10056026:
Testimony of Marge Kilkelly on Behalf of the Maine Council on Aging to the
Committee on Energy, Utilities, and Technology
In Support of LD 1967 Resolve, to Establish the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot Program
Submitted May 15, 2025
Thank you Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, and Members of the Committee on Energy, Utilities, and Technology.
My name is Marge Kilkelly, and I am a Policy Consultant for the Maine Council on Aging (MCOA) which is a broad, multidisciplinary network of over 140 organizations, businesses, municipalities, and older community members working to ensure we can all live healthy, engaged, and secure lives with choices and opportunities as we age at home and in community settings. The MCOA is a unifying force across sectors that is creating a new narrative about aging and older people in Maine with the goal of building local, statewide, and national support for the systemic changes needed to support our new longevity.
I am testifying in Favor of LD 1967 Resolve, to Establish the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot Program.
Mainers are living longer than ever before. With a relatively healthy older population, older adults are remaining active in our workforce, leading civic and social organizations, and developing into an impressive volunteer corp.
When older Mainers are able to stay in their communities it not only enhances their quality of life but also provides benefits to the community. Age-integrated communities create a sense of belonging, fostering stronger social bonds and a more cohesive society. They create opportunities for older adults to serve as mentors and role models. The interactions between community members can help break down age stereotypes lead us to a future without ageism. Age-integrated communities also result in better health outcomes, more community involvement, and decreased loneliness for older individuals.
While nearly all older people want to age in their homes for as long as possible, many older Mainers come to the point where they realize they must leave their homes because they cannot afford to stay. They're living in homes they struggle to afford and energy costs are often a factor.
A 2024 report Quantifying Maine's Household Energy Burden and Affordability Gap estimated that over 200,000 Maine households are facing unaffordable home energy burdens. While this burden is especially true for low income households, even moderate income households face home energy gaps of nearly $700. 29% of older Mainers live in low income families. Improving home energy efficiency result in cost savings that can impact the entire quality of life.
For those on Social Security in 2024 the average benefit was $1,900.00 per month. About a third of all older Mainers live on Social Security alone, with no other retirement benefits. However, many Mainers,

especially women, receive less because of working part time, being a stay at home parent, a caregiver, or earning relatively low incomes in working years. Older women who live alone are more likely impacted by the rising energy costs. In 2022, the Muskie School of Public Service published a data report on the Economic Security of Older Women in Maine, prepared for the Maine Women's Lobby Educational Fund and the Maine Council on Aging.1 This report documents the devastating impacts of lifelong economic gender disparity on older women in Maine and nationally. Specifically, the report shows that more than half of the 50,000 Maine women (65+) who live alone do not have enough money to meet their basic needs, as determined by the Elder Economic Standard Security Index (the Elder Index). The Elder Index finds that an older Mainer in good health living in a home she owns without a mortgage needs a monthly income of $2,110 just to meet her basic needs. While many older homeowners are aware that they need to make improvements, there are lots of questions. What do I need to make my home warmer? Who provides these services? Are there programs available to help with the costs? Which project should I do first? Who can I trust to provide the best information? For too many people, the lack of answers to these questions leaves them either not feeling confident enough to do home weatherization improvements or discovering that the money they have spent has not addressed their most critical need. LD 1967 creates the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot Program an innovative program to address these questions and more. By performing home energy assessments, educating consumers about energy saving opportunities, providing information about financial support and even assisting in analyzing contractor recommendations the staff are living into the definitions of Navigator and Coach which are both needed in the complicated world of energy efficiency. I urge you to support LD 1967 to support older people who want to stay in their homes and continue to support and participate in their communities.
1 https://mainecouncilonaging.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Economic-Security-Older-Women-in-MaineReport-FINAL.pdf

Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, and Members of the Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology, I am testifying on behalf of the Efficiency Maine Trust (the Trust) neither for nor against LD
1967.
As a general matter, the Trust supports efforts from civil society to complement and enhance the
marketplace for home energy improvement projects. To assist such efforts, and to help develop the
marketplace itself, the Trust has been successful in providing complementary resources, including extensive information resources (both online, in print, and in person), workforce training, marketing, rebates and loans.
The Trust has no objection to community-based initiatives that seek to facilitate home improvement
projects. That said, it is not an activity the Trust would fund itself. Dear members of the Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology,

I'm writing to express my support for LD 1967, "Resolve, to Establish the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot Program". I write in my capacity as director of retrofitMAINE, an initiative of the nonprofit passivhausMAINE. My work is predominantly focused on supporting residents in both Freeport and Lewiston, especially those of low- and moderate-income levels, as they seek to make their home more comfortable and affordable.

It is a familiar refrain that Maine has old housing stock - over a third of our homes are older than 1960. As we see by comparison with our improving building standards, our older housing stock does not come without its challenges. These challenges, however, can be overcome. Residents having more affordable monthly utility bills is a realistic and natural result of efficiency-focused home upgrades. Unfortunately, though, most residents I've had the opportunity to interact with simply don't have the capacity to become experts in building science and energy efficiency and then act as their own contractor to complete these upgrades. Residents would also have to understand which upgrades would be worth their investment and further be able to organize this into a prioritized master plan - and somehow find all the grants, rebates, incentives, and financing options for which they may be eligible.

Clearly, there's a lot involved. There are many energy coach/navigator efforts across the state trying to fill this need but we're unable to have the necessary impact as we struggle with multiple challenges. Many communities and organizations attempting to start programs like this have yet to overcome the barriers. retrofitMAINE's program is newer but has been able to launch largely because of our community-engaged approach, partnering with community-based organizations like our local rotary club, community services, and CAP agencies. These partnerships help us support each other and extend our reach and capabilities, but we're still limited in our capacity and funding with the extent of this need. All of us hear the concern and overwhelm from residents and, while retrofitMAINE's coaching program is new, I've already heard appreciation for its existence and how people weren't aware of these upgrades or incentives.

There really is a lot involved in making Maine homes more livable and affordable, but coaching programs like that of retrofitMAINE and many others reduce this burden on residents and could make a significant dent in the state's emissions as we help people recognize and achieve the benefits of decarbonization or other better building practices. It is only through this effort and others like it that we can ensure the goals outlined in Maine Won't Wait are truly feasible.

In order to increase the efficiency, reach, and impact of these navigator and coaching programs, we need the consistency and prioritized funding that a statewide pilot's oversight will provide. I hope this Committee will strongly recommend passing LD 1967.

Thank you for your consideration, Mikaela Heming mika@passivhausMAINE.org

10055891:
Testimony of Rene Augustus La Casse in Support of LD 1967: Resolve, to Establish the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot
Program
Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, and honorable members of the Energy, Utilities, and Technology Committee. I am Rene Augustus La Casse, and I am the Manager of Municipal Strategy and Policy Analyst at A Climate to Thrive (ACTT). ACTT is a community-driven non-profit that is working on a clean energy transition that prioritizes community benefits across Maine, with a particular focus on energy equity. Thank you for providing me with this opportunity to support LD 1967: Resolve, to Establish the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot Program.
This legislation seeks to create the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot Navigator Program which will be overseen by the Office of Community Affairs. This program will provide Maine homeowners with impartial education and analysis about energy-saving opportunities, as well as home assessments of home building performance. The program will function by working with two to five non-profit organizations around Maine to assess the effectiveness of their program, and understand consumer feedback of these programs.
This bill seeks to replicate efforts that have already proven successful. For example, York has implemented a volunteer-powered energy coaching program which has resulted in hundreds of visits by a devoted team of coaches who help homeowners navigate the overwhelming amount of information available to support identification of applicable home performance solutions and available funding to support implementation.. In Massachusetts, the HeatSmart Alliance program has been instrumental in assisting thousands of homeowners in over fifty towns by providing clear information and support to help homeowners access heat pump installation.
At A Climate to Thrive, we have implemented several "Weatherize" and "Electrify" programs over the years to support homeowner insulation, air sealing, and heat pump installation. We have heard time and again that the value in this programs is the clear information they provide to help homeowners navigate what otherwise feels like an overwhelming system and process in terms of understanding available improvements, identifying contractors, and understanding available incentives. In our work throughout the state, we have heard repeated requests from all corners of Maine for a program like the one outlined in this bill. In fact, the need for such a program was referenced in the recommendations made by both the Buildings Working Group and the Energy Working Group during the recent update to Maine Won't Wait, the state climate action plan. ACTT has also heard from numerous organizations throughout the state who are eager to implement this type of energy navigator program, but are unable to do so due to a lack of

funding. This bill would address this funding challenge and accelerate critical, cost-saving building improvements throughout the state.
While heat pumps are an important building performance solution, this bill does well to center building science in the program's construction.This is critical, as foundational solutions like insulation or window improvements are often essential first steps, particularly here in Maine where we have one of the oldest housing stocks in the country. Coaching can illuminate these important steps, supporting homeowners in taking impactful, lasting action.
At a time when many homeowners are struggling to pay their heating bills, a program like this would have lasting, profound impact. This bill will help homeowners learn about minor and major changes they can make to their home that will save them energy and money. ACTT encourages this honorable committee to support LD 1967: Resolve, to Establish the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot Program.
10055853:
Rozanna Patane York LD 1967
I am testifying today in support of LD 1967 "Resolve, to Establish the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot Program." This bill can build on the efforts of several Maine communities that have already demonstrated that energy coach programs are a key component of decarbonizing Maine's homes.
It's a complex process, electrifying and insulating a home, and most homeowners don't know where to start. That's what coaches do, walk people through the process from start to finish, whether the homeowner just wants to install a heat pump or do a major energy retrofit. We help them clarify their goals, get answers to their questions, refer them to professional installers, explain the changing structure of financial incentives, and keep the process moving.
As a member of York Ready for Climate Action, I developed our energy coach program in 2022, adapting the Heatsmart Alliance heat pump model in Massachusetts. A Maine Community Resilience Partnership grant in 2023 helped launch the program and today our 9 volunteer coaches have helped York homeowners transform their homes with nearly 150 installations, including energy audits, insulation, heat pumps, solar, window inserts, and other electrification projects.
As other Maine communities have contacted us, I've helped them establish their own energy coach programs and I've worked with a small group of individuals across the state to develop a statewide model and budget - members of A Climate To Thrive, passivhausMaine, College of the Atlantic, York Ready for Climate Action, Resilience Works, Southern Maine Planning and Development Commission, and others have collaborated on the vision for a statewide energy coach model.
I agree with Michael Stoddard that such a program would be an important component of the State's heat pump accelerator program and more generally, of its efforts to implement the State's climate action plan, Maine Won't Wait.
I trust that the Energy Utilities and Technology Committee will issue a strong recommendation to the legislature to pass LD 1967.
Thank you for the chance to testify in support of LD1967.

10055936:
Paul Perkins John Zittel Bath LD 1967
We are Paul Perkins and John Zittel, both longtime residents of Bath and co-chairs of the City of Bath Climate Action Commission. We are testifying today in support of LD 1967, "Resolve, to Establish the Maine Home Energy Navigator and Coaching Pilot Program".
Bath's Climate Action Commission helped to get an updated Climate Action Plan passed by our City Council last November. Bath's plan, along with a previous City Council Resolution, aligns closely with the goals of the state climate plan, Maine Won't Wait, and seeks to lower our carbon emissions 80% by 2050, a target broadly accepted climate scientists as necessary to avoid the worst climate outcomes.
There is strong demand in Bath for support of the kind envisioned in LD 1967. When we hold public events, the single most frequent question we hear is a variation on: "How can I get help in understanding the choices and options to enable me to make sustainability improvements in my residence?" According to Bath's recent greenhouse gas inventory, our residential sector accounts for 27% of carbon emissions by the City. Reducing those emissions is a daunting task, since old building stock can have a myriad of issues often needing careful and expert assessment. As an illustrative example, consider that building science makes it clear that "improvements" such as air sealing and insulation without understanding of and attention to moisture movement can lead to destructive repercussions.
